notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Nuclear physics deals with the atomic nucleus, its constituents, properties and reactions.
  • The nucleus occupies a very small part of an atom's volume.
  • Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
  • The nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
  • Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons.
  • Electrons exist outside the nucleus.
  • Nuclear forces hold nucleons together.
  • Nuclear reactions involve much larger energies than ordinary chemical reactions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nucleus → Protons + Neutrons

2. Structure of an Atom
  • An atom consists of a positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons.
  • The nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
  • Proton has positive charge.
  • Electron has negative charge.
  • Neutron has no net electric charge.
  • A neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons.
3. Proton
  • Proton is positively charged.
  • Charge of proton = +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Proton mass is approximately 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
  • Proton is located in the nucleus.
  • Number of protons determines the chemical element.
  • Proton number is called atomic number.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Atomic Number → Number of Protons

4. Neutron
  • Neutron has no net electric charge.
  • Neutron mass is approximately 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
  • Neutron is slightly heavier than proton.
  • Neutrons are present in almost all ordinary nuclei except the common hydrogen-1 nucleus.
  • James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

James Chadwick → Neutron → 1932

5. Electron
  • Electron has negative charge.
  • Electron charge = −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Electron mass is approximately 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
  • Electron is much lighter than proton or neutron.
  • J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

J. J. Thomson → Electron → 1897

6. Atomic Number
  • Atomic number is represented by Z.
  • Z = Number of protons.
  • In a neutral atom, Z also equals number of electrons.
  • Every element has a unique atomic number.
  • Hydrogen has atomic number 1.
  • Helium has atomic number 2.
7. Mass Number
  • Mass number is represented by A.
  • A = Number of protons + Number of neutrons.
  • A = Z + N.
  • N represents number of neutrons.
  • Number of neutrons N = A − Z.
  • Mass number is always a whole number.
📌 Must-Memorise

A = Z + N

8. Nuclide Notation

A nuclide is commonly represented as:

  • ᴬZX.
  • X represents chemical symbol.
  • A is mass number.
  • Z is atomic number.

Example:

  • Carbon-14 has A = 14 and Z = 6.
  • Number of neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8.
9. Nucleons
  • Protons and neutrons are collectively called nucleons.
  • Mass number equals the total number of nucleons.
  • Nuclear forces act primarily between nucleons.
10. Nuclear Size
  • Nuclear radius is of the order of 10⁻¹⁵ m.
  • One femtometre equals 10⁻¹⁵ m.
  • Nuclear radius approximately follows R = R₀A¹/³.
  • R₀ is approximately 1.2 fm.
  • Nuclear density is extremely high.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nuclear Scale → Femtometre

11. Isotopes
  • Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
  • They have the same number of protons.
  • They have different numbers of neutrons.
  • Their chemical properties are generally very similar.
  • Their nuclear properties can differ substantially.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Isotopes → Same Z, Different A

12. Hydrogen Isotopes

The main hydrogen isotopes are:

  • Protium → ¹H.
  • Deuterium → ²H or D.
  • Tritium → ³H or T.
  • Protium has 1 proton and no neutron.
  • Deuterium has 1 proton and 1 neutron.
  • Tritium has 1 proton and 2 neutrons.
  • Tritium is radioactive.
📌 Must-Memorise

Protium → 0 neutron

Deuterium → 1 neutron

Tritium → 2 neutrons

13. Deuterium
  • Deuterium is a stable isotope of hydrogen.
  • Its nucleus contains one proton and one neutron.
  • Deuterium oxide is called heavy water.
  • Heavy water formula is D₂O.
  • Heavy water is used as moderator in some nuclear reactors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heavy Water → D₂O

14. Tritium
  • Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen.
  • Its nucleus contains one proton and two neutrons.
  • Tritium undergoes beta decay.
  • Tritium is used in research and fusion-related applications.
15. Isobars
  • Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
  • They belong to different elements.
  • Example: Carbon-14 and Nitrogen-14 have the same mass number 14.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Isobars → Same A, Different Z

16. Isotones
  • Isotones have the same number of neutrons but different atomic numbers.
  • They are different elements.
  • Example: Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons and Nitrogen-15 also has 8 neutrons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Isotones → Same Neutron Number

17. Nuclear Isomers
  • Nuclear isomers are nuclei with the same numbers of protons and neutrons but different nuclear energy states.
  • A metastable nuclear state is indicated by the letter m.
  • Technetium-99m is an important nuclear isomer used in medical imaging.
18. Strong Nuclear Force
  • Strong nuclear interaction is the strongest fundamental interaction.
  • Residual strong nuclear force binds protons and neutrons in nuclei.
  • It acts only over very short nuclear distances.
  • It overcomes electrostatic repulsion between protons at sufficiently small distances.
  • Nuclear force shows approximate charge independence between nucleons in many nuclear models.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Strong Nuclear Force → Holds Nucleus Together

19. Nuclear Stability
  • Nuclear stability depends strongly on the neutron-to-proton ratio.
  • Light stable nuclei generally have approximately equal numbers of neutrons and protons.
  • Heavy stable nuclei require more neutrons than protons.
  • Very heavy nuclei are generally unstable.
  • Unstable nuclei undergo radioactive decay.
20. Radioactivity
  • Radioactivity is spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei.
  • Radioactive decay produces particles and/or electromagnetic radiation.
  • Radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon.
  • Ordinary temperature and pressure have negligible effect on most nuclear decay rates.
  • Radioactive decay is random for an individual nucleus but statistically predictable for large numbers of nuclei.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Radioactivity → Spontaneous Nuclear Decay

21. Discovery of Radioactivity
  • Henri Becquerel discovered natural radioactivity in 1896.
  • He observed radiation from uranium salts.
  • The SI unit becquerel is named after him.
  • Becquerel shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Marie Curie.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Henri Becquerel → Radioactivity → 1896

22. Marie and Pierre Curie
  • Marie Curie and Pierre Curie conducted major studies of radioactivity.
  • They discovered polonium and radium in 1898.
  • Polonium was named after Poland.
  • Radium is highly radioactive.
  • Marie Curie coined and popularised the term radioactivity.
  • Marie Curie received Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Curie → Polonium + Radium

23. Rutherford and Radioactivity
  • Ernest Rutherford distinguished alpha and beta radiation in early radioactivity studies.
  • Rutherford later developed the nuclear model of the atom.
  • His gold-foil experiment established the existence of a small dense nucleus.
  • Rutherford is strongly associated with nuclear physics.
24. Alpha Radiation
  • Alpha particle is the nucleus of helium-4.
  • It contains two protons and two neutrons.
  • Alpha particle carries charge +2e.
  • Alpha radiation has relatively high ionising power.
  • Alpha radiation has low penetrating power.
  • It can be stopped by paper or the outer dead layer of skin.
  • Alpha radiation is strongly deflected by electric and magnetic fields compared with gamma rays.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Alpha → 2p + 2n → +2 Charge

25. Alpha Decay

During alpha decay:

  • Mass number decreases by 4.
  • Atomic number decreases by 2.
  • A new element is formed.

Example pattern:

  • ᴬZX → ᴬ⁻⁴Z⁻²Y + ⁴₂He.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alpha Decay → A − 4, Z − 2

26. Beta Radiation
  • Beta radiation consists of high-speed electrons or positrons emitted in nuclear decay.
  • Beta-minus radiation consists of electrons.
  • Beta-plus radiation consists of positrons.
  • Beta radiation has intermediate ionising power.
  • Beta radiation has greater penetration than alpha but less than gamma.
  • Thin aluminium can stop many beta particles.
27. Beta-Minus Decay
  • In beta-minus decay, a neutron transforms into a proton.
  • An electron and an antineutrino are emitted.
  • Mass number remains unchanged.
  • Atomic number increases by 1.
📌 Must-Memorise

β⁻ Decay → A Same, Z + 1

28. Beta-Plus Decay
  • In beta-plus decay, a proton converts into a neutron.
  • A positron and a neutrino are emitted.
  • Mass number remains unchanged.
  • Atomic number decreases by 1.
📌 Must-Memorise

β⁺ Decay → A Same, Z − 1

29. Positron
  • Positron is the antiparticle of the electron.
  • It has the same mass as an electron.
  • It carries positive elementary charge.
  • Positron is represented as e⁺ or β⁺.
  • Positrons are used indirectly in PET imaging.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Positron → Positive Electron Antiparticle

30. Gamma Radiation
  • Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from nuclei.
  • Gamma rays have no mass and no electric charge.
  • They travel at the speed of light in vacuum.
  • They have very high penetrating power.
  • They have lower ionising power per unit path than alpha particles.
  • Dense materials such as lead or thick concrete are used for shielding.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gamma → Electromagnetic → No Mass, No Charge

31. Gamma Decay
  • Gamma emission usually occurs when an excited nucleus loses excess energy.
  • Mass number does not change.
  • Atomic number does not change.
  • The nucleus moves to a lower energy state.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gamma → A Same, Z Same

32. Alpha–Beta–Gamma Comparison
  • Alpha has highest ionising power among the three in typical comparisons.
  • Gamma has highest penetrating power.
  • Alpha has lowest penetrating power.
  • Beta has intermediate penetration and ionisation.
  • Alpha is positively charged.
  • Beta may be negatively or positively charged.
  • Gamma is uncharged.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ionisation → α > β > γ

Penetration → γ > β > α

33. Deflection in Electric Field
  • Alpha particles are deflected toward the negative plate.
  • Beta-minus particles are deflected toward the positive plate.
  • Beta particles deflect more strongly than alpha because of much smaller mass.
  • Gamma rays are not deflected because they carry no charge.
34. Radioactive Decay Law
  • Number of undecayed nuclei decreases exponentially with time.
  • N = N₀e⁻λt.
  • λ is decay constant.
  • The decay rate at any instant is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

N = N₀e⁻λt

35. Decay Constant
  • Decay constant is represented by λ.
  • It gives the probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay.
  • Larger decay constant means faster radioactive decay.
  • SI unit is s⁻¹.
36. Activity
  • Activity is the number of nuclear decays per second.
  • Activity A = λN.
  • SI unit is becquerel.
  • 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
  • Activity decreases exponentially with time for a single radionuclide.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 Bq = 1 Decay/s

37. Curie
  • Curie is an older non-SI unit of radioactivity.
  • Symbol is Ci.
  • 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.
  • It was historically related to the activity of approximately one gram of radium-226.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq

38. Half-Life
  • Half-life is the time required for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
  • It is represented by T₁/₂.
  • After one half-life, 1/2 remains.
  • After two half-lives, 1/4 remains.
  • After three half-lives, 1/8 remains.
  • Half-life is characteristic of a radionuclide.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

After n Half-Lives → Fraction Remaining = (1/2)ⁿ

39. Half-Life and Decay Constant
  • T₁/₂ = ln2/λ.
  • T₁/₂ ≈ 0.693/λ.
  • Larger λ means shorter half-life.
📌 Must-Memorise

T₁/₂ = 0.693/λ

40. Mean Life
  • Mean life is the average lifetime of a radioactive nucleus.
  • Mean life τ = 1/λ.
  • T₁/₂ = 0.693τ.
  • Mean life is longer than half-life.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mean Life = 1/λ

41. Carbon-14
  • Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope of carbon.
  • It contains 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
  • Carbon-14 undergoes beta decay.
  • Its half-life is approximately 5730 years.
  • It is used in radiocarbon dating.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

C-14 Half-Life → About 5730 Years

42. Radiocarbon Dating
  • Radiocarbon dating estimates the age of once-living organic material.
  • Carbon-14 is used.
  • It is useful mainly for archaeological and relatively recent geological samples.
  • It is not the preferred method for determining the age of Earth.
  • Willard Libby developed radiocarbon dating.
  • Libby received the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Willard Libby → Carbon Dating

43. Uranium-238 Dating
  • Uranium-238 has a very long half-life.
  • Uranium-lead dating is used for very old rocks and minerals.
  • Zircon crystals are especially useful in uranium-lead dating.
  • Such methods are important in estimating Earth's age.
44. Artificial Radioactivity
  • Artificial radioactivity is radioactivity induced in otherwise stable nuclei by nuclear reactions.
  • Frédéric Joliot-Curie and Irène Joliot-Curie discovered artificial radioactivity in 1934.
  • They received the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Joliot-Curies → Artificial Radioactivity → 1934

45. Nuclear Transmutation
  • Nuclear transmutation is conversion of one element or isotope into another through nuclear processes.
  • It can occur naturally through radioactive decay.
  • It can also be induced artificially using particle bombardment.
46. Rutherford's Artificial Transmutation
  • Rutherford performed an early artificial nuclear transmutation experiment in 1919.
  • Alpha particles were used to bombard nitrogen.
  • This resulted in formation of oxygen and emission of a proton.
  • It was an important milestone in nuclear physics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rutherford → Artificial Transmutation → 1919

47. Nuclear Mass
  • Nuclear mass is slightly less than the sum of the masses of its separated constituent nucleons.
  • The difference is called mass defect.
  • Mass defect corresponds to nuclear binding energy.
48. Mass Defect
  • Mass defect = Sum of masses of separate nucleons − Actual nuclear mass.
  • It is represented by Δm.
  • Mass defect is converted into binding energy according to E = mc².
  • Greater mass defect corresponds to greater total binding energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mass Defect → Binding Energy

49. Einstein's Mass–Energy Relation
  • E = mc².
  • Albert Einstein established mass-energy equivalence.
  • c is speed of light.
  • c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • A small mass corresponds to a very large amount of energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Einstein → E = mc²

50. Atomic Mass Unit
  • Atomic mass unit is represented by u.
  • 1 u is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
  • 1 u ≈ 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
  • The energy equivalent of 1 u is approximately 931.5 MeV.
📌 Must-Memorise

1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV/c²

51. Electronvolt
  • Electronvolt is a unit of energy.
  • 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
  • 1 keV = 10³ eV.
  • 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV.
  • 1 GeV = 10⁹ eV.
  • Nuclear energies are commonly measured in MeV.
52. Binding Energy
  • Binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus completely into its nucleons.
  • It is also the energy released when the nucleus is formed from free nucleons.
  • Binding energy = Δmc².
  • Higher total binding energy generally means more energy is needed to break the nucleus apart.
53. Binding Energy per Nucleon
  • Binding energy per nucleon is a measure of average nuclear binding.
  • It increases for light nuclei up to the iron/nickel region.
  • It decreases gradually for very heavy nuclei.
  • This explains why both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei can release energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Highest Stability Region → Iron/Nickel Region

54. Nuclear Fission
  • Nuclear fission is splitting of a heavy nucleus into two or more lighter nuclei.
  • Fission releases large amounts of energy.
  • Neutrons are usually released.
  • Uranium-235 is an important fissile isotope.
  • Plutonium-239 is also fissile.
  • Fission can produce a chain reaction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fission → Heavy Nucleus Splits

55. Discovery of Nuclear Fission
  • Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann experimentally identified nuclear fission products in 1938.
  • Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch provided the physical interpretation of nuclear fission.
  • Fission became a foundation of nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hahn + Strassmann → Fission Experiment

Meitner + Frisch → Interpretation

56. Fission of Uranium-235
  • A slow neutron can be absorbed by uranium-235.
  • The resulting excited uranium nucleus becomes unstable.
  • It splits into two lighter nuclei.
  • Additional neutrons are emitted.
  • Roughly 200 MeV of energy is released per fission event.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

U-235 Fission → ~200 MeV

57. Chain Reaction
  • Neutrons released from one fission can trigger additional fissions.
  • This sequence is called a chain reaction.
  • A controlled chain reaction occurs in a nuclear reactor.
  • An uncontrolled rapidly growing chain reaction can release energy explosively.
58. Critical Mass
  • Critical mass is the minimum amount of fissile material needed under specified conditions to sustain a chain reaction.
  • It depends on geometry, density, purity and neutron losses.
  • Below critical conditions, the reaction dies out.
  • At criticality, a steady chain reaction can be maintained.
59. Nuclear Reactor
  • A nuclear reactor maintains a controlled nuclear fission chain reaction.
  • Heat generated in fission is removed by coolant.
  • Heat can produce steam.
  • Steam rotates turbines.
  • Turbines drive electrical generators.
  • Nuclear energy is thereby converted into electrical energy.
📌 Energy Chain

Nuclear → Thermal → Mechanical → Electrical

60. Main Components of a Nuclear Reactor

Important components include:

  • Nuclear fuel.
  • Moderator in many reactor types.
  • Control rods.
  • Coolant.
  • Reactor vessel/core.
  • Shielding.
  • Heat exchanger or steam generator where applicable.
61. Nuclear Fuel

Common fissile fuels include:

  • Uranium-235.
  • Plutonium-239.
  • Uranium-233.
  • Natural uranium contains mostly uranium-238 and a small fraction of uranium-235.
  • Fuel choice depends on reactor design.
62. Moderator
  • Moderator slows fast neutrons.
  • Slow or thermal neutrons have a high probability of causing U-235 fission.
  • Heavy water can serve as moderator.
  • Ordinary water can serve as moderator.
  • Graphite can serve as moderator.
  • Moderator should slow neutrons without absorbing too many of them.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Moderator → Slows Neutrons

63. Control Rods
  • Control rods absorb neutrons.
  • They regulate the rate of the chain reaction.
  • Boron is used in neutron-absorbing materials.
  • Cadmium is also a strong neutron absorber.
  • Inserting control rods reduces reactor power.
  • Full insertion can shut down the chain reaction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Control Rod → Absorbs Neutrons

64. Coolant
  • Coolant removes heat from the reactor core.
  • Water may serve as coolant.
  • Heavy water may serve as coolant in some reactors.
  • Carbon dioxide has been used in some reactor designs.
  • Liquid sodium is used in some fast reactors.
  • Coolant transfers heat for steam production or further heat exchange.
65. Shielding
  • Reactor shielding reduces exposure to neutrons and gamma radiation.
  • Thick concrete is widely used.
  • Dense materials can reduce gamma radiation.
  • Hydrogen-rich materials are useful in slowing neutrons.
  • Radiation shielding is an essential reactor-safety feature.
66. Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor
  • PHWR stands for Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor.
  • Heavy water is commonly used as moderator and coolant.
  • PHWRs can use natural uranium fuel in suitable designs.
  • PHWR technology is an important part of India's nuclear-power programme.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PHWR → Heavy Water

67. Pressurised Water Reactor
  • PWR stands for Pressurised Water Reactor.
  • Ordinary light water serves as coolant and moderator.
  • Water is kept under high pressure so it does not boil in the primary circuit.
  • Heat is transferred to a secondary system to produce steam.
68. Boiling Water Reactor
  • BWR stands for Boiling Water Reactor.
  • Water boils directly in the reactor vessel.
  • Generated steam drives the turbine.
  • Ordinary water serves as moderator and coolant.
69. Fast Breeder Reactor
  • Fast breeder reactors use fast neutrons.
  • They do not require a conventional neutron moderator.
  • They can produce more fissile material from fertile material under suitable conditions.
  • Uranium-238 can be converted into plutonium-239.
  • Thorium-232 can ultimately be used to breed uranium-233 through appropriate nuclear transformations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Breeder Reactor → Produces Fissile Fuel from Fertile Material

70. Fertile Material
  • Fertile material is not itself readily fissile with thermal neutrons but can be converted into fissile material.
  • Uranium-238 is fertile.
  • Thorium-232 is fertile.
  • U-238 can breed Pu-239.
  • Th-232 can breed U-233.
📌 Must-Memorise

U-238 → Pu-239

Th-232 → U-233

71. Nuclear Fusion
  • Fusion is combination of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
  • Fusion releases enormous energy.
  • Fusion powers the Sun and stars.
  • Fusion requires extremely high temperature.
  • At high temperature, matter exists as plasma.
  • Controlled fusion is technologically difficult.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fusion → Light Nuclei Combine

72. Fusion in the Sun
  • The Sun produces energy mainly by fusion of hydrogen into helium.
  • Proton-proton chain is the dominant fusion process in the Sun.
  • Some mass is converted into energy.
  • The energy ultimately reaches Earth as electromagnetic radiation.
73. Deuterium–Tritium Fusion

A major fusion reaction studied is:

  • Deuterium + Tritium → Helium-4 + Neutron + Energy.
  • D-T fusion releases about 17.6 MeV.
  • Very high temperatures are required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

D + T → He + n + 17.6 MeV

74. Fission vs Fusion
  • Fission splits heavy nuclei.
  • Fusion combines light nuclei.
  • Fission is used in existing commercial nuclear reactors.
  • Fusion powers stars.
  • Both release nuclear energy.
  • Fusion produces more energy per unit mass than ordinary chemical reactions and can exceed fission in specific fuel comparisons.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Reactor today → Mainly Fission

Sun → Fusion

75. Nuclear Reactor vs Atomic Bomb
  • A reactor controls the chain reaction.
  • Control rods and engineered systems regulate neutron population.
  • A nuclear explosive involves an uncontrolled, extremely rapid release of nuclear energy.
  • A power reactor is designed to extract heat gradually.
76. Radiation Detector — Geiger-Müller Counter
  • Geiger-Müller counter detects ionising radiation.
  • It contains a gas-filled tube.
  • Radiation ionises gas inside the tube.
  • Electrical pulses are counted.
  • It can detect alpha, beta and gamma radiation depending on detector design and window.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Geiger Counter → Detects Radiation

77. Cloud Chamber
  • A cloud chamber makes paths of charged particles visible.
  • Ionising particles create ions in supersaturated vapour.
  • Droplets condense along particle tracks.
  • Different particles can produce characteristic track patterns.
78. Scintillation Counter
  • Scintillation detectors produce flashes of light when radiation deposits energy.
  • Photodetectors convert the flashes into electrical signals.
  • They are used in nuclear physics and medical imaging.
79. Dosimeter
  • A dosimeter measures accumulated radiation exposure.
  • Personnel working with radiation may wear dosimeters.
  • Thermoluminescent dosimeters and electronic dosimeters are examples.
80. Absorbed Dose
  • Absorbed radiation dose is energy deposited per unit mass.
  • SI unit is gray.
  • 1 gray = 1 joule per kilogram.
  • Symbol is Gy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gray → Absorbed Dose

81. Equivalent / Effective Dose
  • Sievert is used for radiation doses weighted for biological effect.
  • Symbol is Sv.
  • Biological effect depends on radiation type and exposed tissue.
  • Sievert is important in radiation protection.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sievert → Biological Radiation Effect

82. Roentgen
  • Roentgen is an older unit associated with exposure to X-rays and gamma rays in air.
  • Modern SI radiation-protection quantities use gray and sievert.
  • It is named after Wilhelm Röntgen.
83. Becquerel vs Gray vs Sievert
  • Becquerel → Radioactive activity.
  • Gray → Energy absorbed per kilogram.
  • Sievert → Biological effect/risk-weighted dose.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bq ≠ Gy ≠ Sv

84. Ionising Radiation

Ionising radiation includes:

  • Alpha particles.
  • Beta particles.
  • Gamma rays.
  • X-rays.
  • High-energy neutrons and other particles.
  • Ionising radiation can remove electrons from atoms.
  • Excessive exposure can damage biological tissue.
85. Non-Ionising Radiation

Examples include:

  • Radio waves.
  • Microwaves.
  • Infrared.
  • Visible light.
  • Lower-energy ultraviolet categories are often classified as non-ionising, though UV can still cause chemical and biological damage.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ionising ability depends on photon/particle energy, not simply whether radiation is “electromagnetic”.

86. Biological Effects of Radiation
  • Ionising radiation can damage DNA.
  • High doses can kill cells.
  • Radiation can increase cancer risk.
  • Rapidly dividing tissues are generally more radiosensitive.
  • Radiation effects depend on dose, dose rate, radiation type and exposed tissue.
87. Radiation Protection

Three basic principles are:

  • Reduce exposure time.
  • Increase distance from source.
  • Use appropriate shielding.
📌 Must-Memorise

Time ↓

Distance ↑

Shielding ↑

88. Inverse-Square Radiation Principle
  • For an approximately point-like source without significant absorption, intensity decreases roughly as 1/r².
  • Doubling distance reduces intensity to approximately one-fourth.
  • Increasing distance is therefore an effective radiation-protection measure.
89. Shielding for Alpha
  • Alpha particles have low penetration.
  • Paper or skin can stop external alpha radiation.
  • Alpha emitters can be dangerous if inhaled or swallowed because of strong local ionisation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Low external penetration does not mean alpha sources are harmless inside the body.

90. Shielding for Beta
  • Beta radiation can be stopped by thin metal or suitable plastic.
  • Aluminium is commonly used in textbook examples.
  • Shielding must be designed carefully because high-energy beta particles can generate bremsstrahlung X-rays in dense materials.
91. Shielding for Gamma
  • Gamma radiation is highly penetrating.
  • Lead is commonly used as gamma shielding.
  • Thick concrete is also effective.
  • Greater thickness reduces transmitted intensity.
92. Shielding for Neutrons
  • Neutrons are best slowed using materials containing light nuclei such as hydrogen.
  • Water and concrete can provide neutron shielding.
  • Boron-containing materials can absorb slow neutrons.
93. X-Rays vs Gamma Rays
  • Both are electromagnetic radiation.
  • They overlap in energy ranges.
  • Their traditional distinction is based mainly on origin.
  • X-rays usually arise from electronic processes outside the nucleus or bremsstrahlung.
  • Gamma rays arise mainly from nuclear transitions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

X-ray → Electron/atomic origin

Gamma → Nuclear origin

94. Nuclear Medicine
  • Nuclear medicine uses radionuclides for diagnosis and treatment.
  • Small amounts of radioactive tracers can follow physiological processes.
  • Gamma-emitting tracers are commonly used in diagnostic imaging.
  • Therapeutic radionuclides deliver radiation to selected tissues.
95. Technetium-99m
  • Technetium-99m is widely used in diagnostic nuclear medicine.
  • It emits gamma radiation suitable for imaging.
  • Its relatively short half-life helps limit prolonged radiation exposure.
  • It is used in scans of several organs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tc-99m → Medical Diagnostic Imaging

96. Iodine-131
  • Iodine-131 is a radioactive isotope of iodine.
  • The thyroid naturally concentrates iodine.
  • Iodine-131 is used in diagnosis and treatment of certain thyroid conditions.
  • It emits beta and gamma radiation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

I-131 → Thyroid

97. Cobalt-60
  • Cobalt-60 is a radioactive isotope.
  • It emits energetic gamma rays.
  • It has been used in radiotherapy.
  • It is also used in sterilisation and industrial radiography.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Co-60 → Gamma Source

98. PET
  • PET stands for Positron Emission Tomography.
  • PET uses positron-emitting radionuclides.
  • Positron annihilation produces two gamma photons emitted approximately in opposite directions.
  • Detectors reconstruct the distribution of tracer in the body.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PET → Positron Emission

99. Radiation in Cancer Treatment
  • Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation to damage cancer-cell DNA.
  • External-beam radiation may use high-energy X-rays or particles.
  • Some treatments use radioactive sources placed near or inside tumours.
  • Treatment aims to maximise tumour dose while limiting normal-tissue exposure.
100. Sterilisation by Radiation
  • Gamma radiation and electron beams can sterilise certain medical equipment.
  • Radiation destroys microorganisms by damaging biological molecules.
  • It can sterilise sealed products without high-temperature heating.
101. Food Irradiation
  • Food irradiation uses controlled ionising radiation.
  • It can reduce microorganisms, insects and spoilage.
  • Proper irradiation does not make food itself radioactive under normal approved conditions.
  • It can extend shelf life of selected foods.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Irradiated food ≠ Radioactive food.

102. Radioactive Tracers
  • Radioisotopes can be used as tracers.
  • They help study chemical, biological and industrial processes.
  • Tracers can locate leaks in pipelines.
  • They can track nutrient uptake in plants.
  • Medical tracers can show organ function.
103. Industrial Radiography
  • Gamma rays or X-rays can inspect internal defects in welds and castings.
  • The method is non-destructive.
  • Dense defects and material differences affect transmitted radiation.
104. Thickness Measurement
  • Radioisotope gauges can measure thickness of paper, metal sheets and other products.
  • The amount of radiation transmitted depends on material thickness.
  • Such gauges permit continuous industrial monitoring.
105. Smoke Detector
  • Some ionisation-type smoke detectors use americium-241.
  • The radioactive source ionises air.
  • Smoke alters the ionisation current.
  • The detector then triggers an alarm.
  • Other smoke-detector technologies use optical principles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ionisation Smoke Detector → Am-241

106. Cosmic Rays
  • Cosmic rays are high-energy particles arriving from space.
  • Many primary cosmic rays are protons.
  • They interact with Earth's atmosphere to produce secondary particles.
  • Cosmic rays contribute to natural background radiation.
107. Background Radiation

Natural background radiation comes from:

  • Cosmic rays.
  • Radioactive rocks and soil.
  • Radon gas.
  • Naturally occurring radionuclides in the human body and food.
  • Background level varies geographically.
108. Radon
  • Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive noble gas.
  • It forms in decay chains of uranium and thorium.
  • Radon can accumulate in poorly ventilated buildings.
  • Long-term high radon exposure increases lung-cancer risk.
109. Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme of India

India's nuclear programme is designed around long-term use of uranium and thorium resources.

Broad stages are:

  • Stage I → Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors using uranium fuel.
  • Stage II → Fast Breeder Reactors using plutonium and fertile materials.
  • Stage III → Thorium-based systems aimed at utilising uranium-233 bred from thorium-232.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India → Three-Stage Nuclear Programme → Thorium Important

110. Thorium in India
  • India has significant thorium resources.
  • Thorium-232 is fertile, not directly fissile with thermal neutrons.
  • Thorium-232 can ultimately be converted into fissile uranium-233.
  • Thorium utilisation is important in India's long-term nuclear strategy.
  • Monazite sands are an important source of thorium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Thorium → Monazite → U-233 Route

111. Homi J. Bhabha
  • Homi Jehangir Bhabha is regarded as the architect of India's nuclear programme.
  • He played a major role in establishing India's atomic-energy institutions.
  • India's three-stage nuclear strategy is strongly associated with Bhabha's vision.
  • Bhabha Atomic Research Centre is named after him.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Homi J. Bhabha → Indian Nuclear Programme

112. Atomic Energy Commission of India
  • Atomic Energy Commission was established in 1948.
  • It formulates policy relating to atomic-energy development in India.
  • Homi J. Bhabha served as its first chairman.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Atomic Energy Commission → 1948

113. Department of Atomic Energy
  • Department of Atomic Energy is abbreviated DAE.
  • DAE was established in 1954.
  • It administers major nuclear research, power and fuel-cycle institutions in India.
  • DAE functions under the direct charge of the Prime Minister of India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

DAE → 1954

114. Bhabha Atomic Research Centre
  • BARC stands for Bhabha Atomic Research Centre.
  • It is located at Trombay in Mumbai.
  • It is a major multidisciplinary nuclear research centre.
  • It was originally established as the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay.
  • It was later renamed in honour of Homi J. Bhabha.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

BARC → Trombay, Mumbai

115. Apsara
  • Apsara was India's first nuclear research reactor.
  • It achieved criticality in 1956.
  • It was also the first nuclear research reactor in Asia.
  • It was located at Trombay.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Apsara → First Indian/Asian Research Reactor → 1956

116. Tarapur Atomic Power Station
  • Tarapur Atomic Power Station is located in Maharashtra.
  • It was India's first commercial nuclear power station.
  • Its first units began commercial operation in 1969.
  • It is an important historical milestone in Indian nuclear power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Nuclear Power Station in India → Tarapur

117. Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited
  • NPCIL stands for Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited.
  • NPCIL is a Government of India enterprise under the Department of Atomic Energy.
  • It is responsible for nuclear power reactor construction and operation in India.
118. Kalpakkam — Tamil Nadu
  • Kalpakkam is an important nuclear-energy and research centre in Tamil Nadu.
  • It is located on the coast south of Chennai.
  • Madras Atomic Power Station is located at Kalpakkam.
  • Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research is also located at Kalpakkam.
  • Fast-reactor research is strongly associated with Kalpakkam.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kalpakkam → MAPS + IGCAR + Fast Reactor Research

119. Madras Atomic Power Station
  • MAPS stands for Madras Atomic Power Station.
  • It is located at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu.
  • It uses pressurised heavy-water reactor technology.
  • It is one of India's important indigenous nuclear-power stations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

MAPS → Kalpakkam

120. Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research
  • IGCAR stands for Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research.
  • It is located at Kalpakkam.
  • It specialises particularly in fast-reactor science and technology.
  • It is under the Department of Atomic Energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

IGCAR → Kalpakkam → Fast Reactors

121. Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
  • PFBR stands for Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor.
  • It is located at Kalpakkam.
  • It is designed around fast-breeder technology.
  • It is associated with the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme.
  • Fast reactors help utilise plutonium and breed additional fissile material.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PFBR → Kalpakkam → Stage II

122. Kudankulam Nuclear Power Project
  • Kudankulam Nuclear Power Project is located in Tirunelveli district, Tamil Nadu.
  • It was developed with Russian collaboration.
  • It uses VVER-type pressurised water reactor technology.
  • Kudankulam is one of India's major nuclear-power sites.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kudankulam → Tirunelveli → Russian Collaboration → VVER

123. VVER
  • VVER is a Russian-designed pressurised water reactor family.
  • It uses ordinary water as coolant and moderator.
  • Kudankulam reactors are based on VVER technology.
124. Nuclear Energy — Advantages
  • Very high energy density.
  • Low direct carbon dioxide emissions during reactor operation.
  • Large continuous electricity output.
  • Small fuel mass can produce large amounts of energy.
  • It can reduce dependence on fossil fuels.
125. Nuclear Energy — Challenges
  • Radioactive-waste management.
  • High construction and decommissioning costs.
  • Need for strong safety systems.
  • Potential consequences of severe accidents.
  • Nuclear-material security and proliferation concerns.
  • Long project development periods.
126. Radioactive Waste
  • Radioactive waste remains hazardous for different lengths of time depending on radionuclides present.
  • Low-level and high-level wastes require different management.
  • Spent nuclear fuel contains radioactive fission products and actinides.
  • Waste management can involve storage, treatment, reprocessing and geological disposal strategies.
127. Nuclear Reprocessing
  • Reprocessing separates usable nuclear materials from spent fuel.
  • Uranium and plutonium can potentially be recovered.
  • Reprocessing can support closed fuel-cycle strategies.
  • It requires specialised facilities and safeguards.
128. Nuclear Safety — Defence in Depth
  • Nuclear facilities employ multiple safety barriers.
  • Reactor shutdown systems stop the chain reaction.
  • Cooling systems remove decay heat.
  • Containment structures limit release of radioactive material.
  • Redundancy and diversity improve safety.
129. Decay Heat
  • Radioactive fission products continue to release heat even after a reactor is shut down.
  • This is called decay heat.
  • Continued cooling is therefore necessary after shutdown.
  • Decay heat falls gradually with time.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Shutting down fission does not immediately reduce reactor heat production to zero.

130. Nuclear Criticality
  • Subcritical → Neutron population decreases.
  • Critical → Chain reaction remains steady.
  • Supercritical → Neutron population increases.
  • Power reactors operate around controlled critical conditions during steady operation.
131. Nuclear Fusion Confinement

Two broad experimental approaches are:

  • Magnetic confinement.
  • Inertial confinement.
  • Magnetic confinement uses strong magnetic fields to confine plasma.
  • Tokamak is a well-known magnetic-confinement design.
132. Tokamak
  • Tokamak is a toroidal magnetic-confinement device.
  • It confines hot plasma using magnetic fields.
  • It is widely used in fusion research.
  • Fusion plasma cannot be allowed to contact ordinary material walls continuously at full operating temperatures.
133. Nuclear Force vs Electrostatic Force
  • Protons repel each other electrically.
  • Strong nuclear force attracts nucleons over short distances.
  • At nuclear distances, strong interaction can overcome proton-proton electrostatic repulsion.
  • At larger distances, nuclear force falls off rapidly.
134. Nuclear Reaction vs Chemical Reaction
  • Chemical reactions rearrange electrons.
  • Nuclear reactions change the nucleus.
  • Chemical reactions do not normally change one element into another.
  • Nuclear reactions can transmute elements.
  • Nuclear energies are enormously larger per atom than ordinary chemical energies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chemical → Electrons

Nuclear → Nucleus

135. Important Nuclear Units
  • Activity → Becquerel.
  • Absorbed dose → Gray.
  • Effective/equivalent dose → Sievert.
  • Nuclear energy → eV, keV, MeV.
  • Atomic mass → u.
  • Nuclear radius → femtometre.
136. Important Scientist–Discovery Pairs
  • J. J. Thomson → Electron.
  • Ernest Rutherford → Nucleus / alpha-scattering model.
  • James Chadwick → Neutron.
  • Henri Becquerel → Radioactivity.
  • Marie and Pierre Curie → Radium and polonium.
  • Joliot-Curies → Artificial radioactivity.
  • Rutherford → Artificial transmutation.
  • Einstein → Mass-energy equivalence.
  • Hahn and Strassmann → Experimental nuclear fission.
  • Meitner and Frisch → Explanation of nuclear fission.
  • Willard Libby → Radiocarbon dating.
  • Homi J. Bhabha → Indian nuclear programme.
137. Important Dates
  • Electron discovered → 1897.
  • Natural radioactivity discovered → 1896.
  • Polonium and radium discovered → 1898.
  • Rutherford nuclear transmutation → 1919.
  • Neutron discovered → 1932.
  • Artificial radioactivity → 1934.
  • Nuclear fission discovery work → 1938.
  • Atomic Energy Commission of India → 1948.
  • DAE → 1954.
  • Apsara reactor → 1956.
  • Tarapur nuclear power station → 1969.
138. Must-Memorise Decay Changes
  • Alpha → A − 4, Z − 2.
  • Beta minus → A same, Z + 1.
  • Beta plus → A same, Z − 1.
  • Gamma → A same, Z same.
139. Must-Memorise Radiation Comparison
  • Alpha → He nucleus.
  • Beta minus → Electron.
  • Beta plus → Positron.
  • Gamma → Photon.
  • Highest ionisation → Alpha.
  • Highest penetration → Gamma.
  • Alpha shield → Paper.
  • Beta shield → Thin aluminium/plastic.
  • Gamma shield → Lead/thick concrete.
140. TNPSC Traps
  • Nucleus contains protons and neutrons.
  • Hydrogen-1 nucleus contains no neutron.
  • Atomic number equals proton number.
  • Mass number equals protons plus neutrons.
  • Isotopes → Same atomic number, different mass number.
  • Isobars → Same mass number, different atomic number.
  • Isotones → Same neutron number.
  • Radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon.
  • Radioactive decay is spontaneous and statistical.
  • Alpha is a helium nucleus, not an electron.
  • Beta-minus is an electron emitted from nuclear transformation.
  • Gamma is electromagnetic radiation.
  • Gamma has no charge.
  • Alpha has greatest ionising ability in standard comparison.
  • Gamma has greatest penetration.
  • Half-life is not the time for all nuclei to decay.
  • After one half-life, 50% remains.
  • After two half-lives, 25% remains.
  • Carbon-14 is used for once-living materials.
  • Carbon-14 is not used to determine Earth's age.
  • Fission splits heavy nuclei.
  • Fusion combines light nuclei.
  • Sun produces energy by fusion.
  • Commercial nuclear reactors use fission.
  • Moderator slows neutrons.
  • Control rods absorb neutrons.
  • Coolant removes heat.
  • Heavy water formula is D₂O.
  • U-238 and Th-232 are fertile materials.
  • U-235, Pu-239 and U-233 are fissile materials.
  • Gray measures absorbed dose.
  • Sievert reflects biological effect.
  • Becquerel measures activity.
  • Irradiated food is not automatically radioactive.
  • X-rays and gamma rays are distinguished mainly by origin.
  • Alpha radiation can be dangerous inside the body despite weak external penetration.
  • Nuclear reactor shutdown does not immediately eliminate decay heat.
  • India's long-term nuclear programme strongly emphasises thorium.
  • Kalpakkam and Kudankulam are major Tamil Nadu nuclear sites.

  • Proton → Positive.
  • Neutron → Neutral.
  • Electron → Negative.
  • Z → Protons.
  • A → p + n.
  • Isotope → Same Z.
  • Isobar → Same A.
  • Isotone → Same n.
  • Becquerel → Radioactivity.
  • Alpha → He nucleus.
  • Beta → Electron/positron.
  • Gamma → EM radiation.
  • Ionisation → α highest.
  • Penetration → γ highest.
  • Half-life → 50%.
  • C-14 → 5730 years.
  • Activity → Bq.
  • Dose → Gy.
  • Biological dose → Sv.
  • Mass defect → Binding energy.
  • Einstein → E = mc².
  • Fission → Heavy splits.
  • Fusion → Light combines.
  • Reactor → Controlled chain.
  • Moderator → Slows neutrons.
  • Control rod → Absorbs neutrons.
  • Heavy water → D₂O.
  • U-238 → Pu-239.
  • Th-232 → U-233.
  • Sun → Fusion.
  • Bhabha → Indian nuclear programme.
  • Kalpakkam → MAPS + IGCAR.
  • Kudankulam → VVER.
